Fret
FRET
verb
From the Saxon fretan, “to eat away, to devour” (for- + etan, to eat); hence to gnaw, to corrode, to wear away by rubbing — and so, of the mind, to chafe and vex itself. The AV keeps the literal sense in Lev 13:55, “it is fret inward.”

Biblical Definition

To fret is to gnaw — the word is literally a devouring. A garment with the plague in it “is fret inward” (Lev 13:55), eaten away beneath the surface where the eye does not reach; and that is precisely what fretting does to a soul. The great passage is the thirty-seventh Psalm, where David forbids it three times over, and each time attaches the same cause. “Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity” (Psa 37:1). “Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way” (Psa 37:7). “Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil” (Psa 37:8). Solomon repeats it: “Fret not thyself because of evil men, neither be thou envious at the wicked” (Pro 24:19). Mark the diagnosis. Fretting is not first anxiety about tomorrow; it is envy of the prosperous wicked, the corroding suspicion that God has mismanaged the world and that the ungodly have got the better bargain. Asaph confessed the same disease and was cured only in the sanctuary, when he understood their end (Psa 73:17). Note also the reflexive: fret not thyself. A man is his own gnawer. And the cure is not a technique but a Person — rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for Him, for yet a little while and the wicked shall not be.

Webster 1828 Definition

To gnaw or eat away; hence to vex, to chafe, to wear one’s self by discontent.

FRET, to rub; to wear away by friction; to corrode.

To agitate; to vex; to make angry; and intransitively, to be vexed or chafed.

From Saxon fretan, “to eat away, devour” (for- + etan, to eat).

The AV keeps the literal sense of a garment: it is fret inward (Lev 13:55).

David thrice forbids it: fret not thyself (Psa 37:1, 7, 8).

Key Scripture

Psa 37:1 — "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity."

Psa 37:7 — "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass."

Psa 37:8 — "Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil."

Pro 24:19 — "Fret not thyself because of evil men, neither be thou envious at the wicked;"

Modern Corruption

Fretting has been reclassified as a condition to be managed rather than a sin to be mortified — and its root, envy at the prospering wicked, is never named at all.

expand to see more

Our age treats the fretting mind as a medical fact and nothing more: a state to be soothed, a matter for technique, breathing, and distraction. Scripture is far more searching and far more hopeful. It names fretting a sin — it stands in Psa 37 between anger and wrath, and it is forbidden in the imperative — and a sin can be repented of, mortified, and forgiven, which a mere condition cannot. This is not to say every troubled soul is simply rebellious; bodies break, sleep fails, and the LORD deals tenderly with dust, and He knoweth our frame. But the fretting David forbids has a doctrinal root, and no technique will pull it: it is envy at the prosperity of the wicked, which is unbelief about the government of God.

The cure Scripture gives is threefold, and every part of it is theology. First, look at the end: “for they shall soon be cut down like the grass” (Psa 37:2); Asaph could not stop fretting until he went into the sanctuary and understood their latter end. Second, rest in the LORD and wait patiently for Him — the doctrine of providence turned into a posture, believing that not one prospering wicked man escapes the Judge of all the earth. Third, do good and dwell in the land — the psalm answers idle gnawing with active duty, because a man occupied in his calling has less leisure to eat himself. Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and He shall sustain thee (Psa 55:22); the burden was never yours to carry, and the gnawing was never yours to keep.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

To gnaw or eat away; hence to chafe with envy at the prospering wicked.

expand to see more

Fret — Saxon fretan, “to eat away, devour.”

Literal in the AV of a corroded garment: it is fret inward (Lev 13:55).

Reflexive in the Psalms: a man frets himself (Psa 37:1, 7, 8).

Its root is envy at the prosperity of the wicked, not fear of tomorrow.

Its cure is rest in the LORD and patient waiting (Psa 37:7).

Usage

"Fret not thyself because of evildoers — the command is reflexive; the gnawer is oneself."

"It is fret inward: the plague eats the garment where no eye sees, as envy eats the soul."

"Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: providence is the only cure for fretting."
